RCS is measured in square meters (m²) or dBsm (decibels relative to a square meter)
Most modern stealth aircraft have an RCS of less than 0.0002 m²
The B-2 stealth bomber has a head-on RCS comparable to a bird, approximately 0.01 m² or -20 dBm²
A Tomahawk cruise missile has an RCS of less than 0.05 m²
To reduce detection distance to one-tenth, RCS must be reduced by a factor of 10,000
The US AWACS radar was designed to detect aircraft with 7 m² RCS at 370 km range
AWACS can detect typical nonstealthy cruise missiles at 227 km range
AWACS can detect stealthy cruise missiles at only 108 km range
Geometric Optics is valid only when object size is much larger than radar wavelength
Method of Moments divides aircraft surface into patches approximately 1/10 of a wavelength in size
Bistatic RCS is typically larger than monostatic RCS due to multiple receivers
The impedance of free space (η) is approximately 377 Ω
Fifth-generation fighters include F-22, F-35, J-20, and Su-57
Sixth-generation aircraft designs include NGAD, F/A-XX, and PAK DP
The Have Blue was the first stealth aircraft testbed
Stealth aircraft rose to prominence during the Gulf War in 1991
Beyond-visual-range (BVR) combat originated during the Vietnam War
F-117 and B-2 are unstable on three axes and cannot perform supersonic flight
Opening bomb bay doors can more than double an aircraft's radar return
External auxiliary fuel tanks dramatically increase RCS
Radar-absorbent materials (RAM) convert electromagnetic energy into heat, increasing surface temperature
Curved surfaces reflect radar waves in multiple directions, while flat planes reflect in one direction
Purpose shaping directs reflected radar waves away from the incident direction
Plane alignment (facet) design ensures no surfaces are normal to incident radar waves
Active cancellation technology requires very powerful computers and sensitive detectors and emitters
